abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a fundamentally new mathematical framework for hierarchical spline spaces that transcends the limitations of classical multivariate spline theory. We establish that spline spaces on complex domains can be characterized through admissible partitions, where the geometric structure and topological constraints define an intrinsic algebraic system. By developing a theory of nested spline subspaces with explicit connection operators, we prove the existence of locally supported basis functions with optimal approximation properties in arbitrary dimensions. The key innovation lies in reformulating the classical dimension formula as a consequence of homological algebra principles, thereby unifying previously disparate approaches including T-splines, hierarchical B-splines, and trimmed surfaces under a single theoretical umbrella. Our framework reveals that the refinement process in geometric modeling corresponds to a filtered system in algebraic topology, where stability of approximation depends on geometric quality measures. We demonstrate that this paradigm shift enables construction of basis functions with prescribed vanishing moments and controlled support size, addressing long-standing challenges in computer aided geometric design. The theoretical results are validated through explicit constructions on non-trivial topology, establishing foundations for future developments in splines theory and parametric modeling.

We present a refined mathematical analysis of approximation properties for hierarchical B-spline constructions on geometric domains with complex features. While existing error estimates provide asymptotic bounds, they fail to capture the subtle interplay between mesh geometry and approximation quality that determines practical performance. Our approach establishes sharp a priori estimates that explicitly incorporate geometric parameters of the triangulation, including local mesh ratio, element shape quality, and curvature measures of the domain boundary. We prove that the approximation error can be bounded by terms proportional to the condition number of the underlying spline space, yielding estimates that are significantly tighter than classical results for non-quasi-uniform configurations. The analysis reveals that eigenvalue distribution of the stiffness matrix provides a precise characterization of how local refinement affects global approximation power. By introducing novel projection constants that encode geometric anisotropy, we derive optimal convergence rates for both the $L^2$ norm and energy norm that remain valid under highly graded meshes. These theoretical findings explain the empirical success of adaptive refinement strategies in isogeometric analysis and provide rigorous guidance for designing optimal mesh grading in computer aided geometric design applications.

We present a complete framework for adaptive isogeometric analysis that seamlessly integrates hierarchical mesh generation, local error estimation, and solution-driven refinement within a unified computational paradigm. The proposed system introduces a localized refinement strategy that allocates computational resources based on a hierarchical error indicator combining geometric approximation error with discretization error in the numerical solution. By exploiting the inherent continuity properties of T-spline representations, our method achieves $C^1$-smooth approximations across arbitrary refinement hierarchies without requiring constraint solving or remedy patches. The architecture incorporates automatic detection of geometric features including sharp edges, high-curvature regions, and topological handles, enabling targeted refinement that preserves essential shape characteristics. We develop efficient data structures for representing and manipulating hierarchical spline spaces that support both h-refinement and k-refinement operations with guaranteed numerical stability. Implementation details address practical concerns including quadrature rule selection, basis function evaluation, and parallel assembly for large-scale geometric models. Numerical experiments on challenging CAD benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves optimal convergence rates while maintaining geometric fidelity with substantially reduced computational cost compared to uniform refinement approaches, offering a new paradigm for high-fidelity simulation in computer aided geometric design.

We propose an enhanced surface reconstruction pipeline that significantly improves upon existing approaches for converting unorganized point clouds to manifold triangle meshes suitable for geometry processing. The method advances current techniques through three key innovations: a multi-scale covariance analysis for robust local normal estimation that reduces sensitivity to noise and outliers; an adaptive ball-pivoting algorithm with dynamic radius selection guided by local point density and curvature estimates; and a topology-preserving mesh optimization that eliminates common artifacts including holes, self-intersections, and non-manifold vertices without compromising geometric accuracy. The system architecture implements a streaming pipeline that processes massive point sets exceeding available memory through chunked computation and incremental mesh building. We introduce a quality metric combining geometric fidelity, mesh regularity, and computational efficiency that enables automatic parameter selection for diverse input characteristics. Experimental evaluation on standard benchmarks demonstrates substantial improvements: 35% reduction in Hausdorff distance compared to state-of-the-art reconstruction methods, 60% improvement in mesh quality metrics, and 40% reduction in computational time through optimized algorithms and intelligent caching. The reconstructed meshes exhibit excellent properties for downstream applications in shape analysis and computational geometry, with guaranteed manifold structure and controlled element quality suitable for finite element analysis.
